Local Zoo Opens "Two-Way Petting Zoo" So Animals Can Pet You Back

Animal rights activists are calling the exhibit a groundbreaking step toward equality, while the animals involved remain completely unaware that they have joined the movement.

By Jonas & Paula September 17, 2026 3 min read

LOS ANGLES, CA— Zhang Zoo opened a new exhibit called "Two-Way Petting Zoo" this week. Instead of humans petting animals, the animals now get to pet people back. 

"It has never seemed fair before," said zoo director Losa Ruxemburg. "We pet them, stare at them, feed them out of the palms of our hands, we take their pictures. And what do they get from all this? Nothing. So now they finally get something too."

How this works is a visitor kneels down next to an animal, a zoo worker picks up the animals paw or wings and pats the person with it. Creative, right? 

So far, the most popular animal is the big boned (fat) pig named Piggie Smalls. Zoo workers say Smalls has "pet back" more than 420 people this week. Piggie does not seem to realize that this is occurring.

"Honestly, it changed my life," cried visitor Tess Tickle, 25. She was wiping her eyes after a chicken flapped near her. "It really felt like it truly saw me. Like he selected me over every other person."

The unfortunate truth is that the chicken didn't choose her. He was put there by a zookeeper. 

According to the zoo representatives, this idea arose from a lot of "research" into how animals feel about being touched. A sign at the front gate describes it as "a great leap forward for animal consent," although all of the animals in the exhibit are either leashed or behind a fence.

However, not everybody is impressed. The primary opponent is Dr. Ben Dover, who studies animal behavior. "A llama doesn't give a damn about your feelings," he said. "It is being picked up and moved so that it can touch strangers for 8+ hours a day. I am not an expert, but that is definitely not a friendship. That is a full-time job it never consented to do." To counteract this criticism, the zoo erected a small sign by the llama pen: "I Consent." Unfortunately, the llama can't read the sign because it is a llama.

 Surprisingly, the exhibit is functioning oddly well. Since its opening, zoo attendance has increased by 50%. The zoo gift shop sold out of t-shirts reading: "A Goat Pet Me And He Meant It," and the zoo plans to add more. For more future plans, supposedly next spring visitors can pay an additional $12 to have a sea lion "wave hello" (which basically consists of a trainer holding a fish behind the guest's head until the sea lion moves its flipper). The zoo is also planning a "Two-Way Selfie Station," where a giraffe will be guided into position so it looks like it's taking a picture of the guest. Giraffes cannot hold telephones. The giraffe will also not know this is happening. 

"We simply want people to leave the zoo feeling as if the animals connected with them," Dickerson stated. "Whether that connection is actual or not is somewhat irrelevant."
